summary: Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October and youth unemployment rose to 13.7%; Ottawa sells its budget, and Democrats' tariff pledges collide with Trump's veto.
body: Statistics Canada says employment was little changed in October, down 4,700, and the unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, its second rise in a row.[^1] Young people were hit hardest: unemployment for 15- to 24-year-olds rose to 13.7% from 13.0%.[^1][^2] In Ontario the rate rose to 7.3%, mainly because more people were looking for work.[^1] Retail and wholesale lost 29,000 jobs, while construction and education gained.[^1] Economists had expected a gain; CIBC's Avery Shenfeld said the economy is "just not hot enough", which hurts students and young people most, though he does not see a recession yet.[^2][^3]

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne are touring the country to sell Thursday's budget.[^5] With a Liberal majority it is expected to pass even though the Conservatives will vote against it.[^5][^4] It projects a $62.3 billion deficit this year, and interest on the debt now costs more than federal health transfers.[^4] One item for young people: free museum admission for under-25s.[^6]

On trade, Democrats who won the US Congress promise to repeal Trump's tariffs on Canada, but they lack the votes to override his veto, and Trump answered with an image of a hat reading "veto".[^7] Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says Ottawa will "focus on what we can control."[^7] Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told senators that inflation of about 3% is driven mainly by oil prices, and that another rate rise is possible; the next decision is Dec 9.[^8]
differences: Conservatives link federal deficits to higher inflation and rates; Macklem said spending is "not really" adding to inflation, and a Desjardins economist calls the effect slight.[^9] Outlets also total the budget differently, from $142 billion in new measures to $151 billion in added spending.[^4][^6]
